chapter_title: Creational Patterns: Factory Method and Abstract Factory

screens.title: Creational Patterns: Factory Method & Abstract Factory
screens.subtitle: Decouple object creation so your code stays flexible, testable, and open to extension.

narration.text: In this lesson we focus on creational design patterns that solve a single recurring problem: how to create objects without tightly coupling client code to concrete classes. You will learn the intent of the Factory Method and the Abstract Factory, see practical Python examples, and get a short hands-on task you can implement. We begin with the real-world problem of a document editor that needs to support many document types without littering client code with type checks. Then we move to a cross-platform GUI factory that must produce consistent component families. Along the way we highlight common mistakes, like instantiating concrete classes everywhere or forgetting to make factory methods abstract. By the end you will be able to choose between creating a single product via a Factory Method or producing coordinated families of products via an Abstract Factory. Think about how this reduces maintenance when new types appear, and how it helps adhere to the Open/Closed Principle. Ready to explore how factories make your Python code more modular and extensible?

keyIdea.title: Make object creation a responsibility, not a dependency
keyIdea.text: Use Factory Method to delegate single-product creation; use Abstract Factory to create families of related products without referencing concrete classes.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Creational Patterns Overview

Factory Method & Abstract Factory

Patterns that centralize creation rules so the rest of your code asks for behavior, not types.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson

Understand why decoupling creation helps maintainability, implement Factory Method with a document example, build an Abstract Factory for UI components, and practice with a logger factory exercise.

Why it matters

When new types arrive, factories let you extend behavior without changing client code, honoring the Open/Closed Principle and reducing bugs caused by scattered instantiation logic.

Outcome

You will be able to pick and implement the appropriate creational pattern and avoid common pitfalls when extending systems with new product types.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical competencies. First, you will explain the problem creational patterns solve: decoupling clients from concrete classes so systems are easier to extend. Second, you will contrast direct instantiation with pattern-driven creation, recognizing the maintenance costs of scattered new statements. Third, you will implement the Factory Method in Python to delegate instantiation to subclasses, and you will run a small example that creates documents without the client knowing concrete types. Fourth, you will implement an Abstract Factory in Python to produce families of related objects, for example platform-specific buttons and checkboxes, and reason about when that approach is preferable. Each objective includes a small verification milestone so you can self-check that the skill is working. These skills let you design systems that follow the Open/Closed Principle and reduce coupling across modules, which matters when software evolves or when testing and mocking are required.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Checks
screens.subtitle: Concrete verification and common pitfalls to avoid

narration.text: These objectives also include practical checks and warnings. When you implement a factory, confirm that client code does not import or instantiate concrete products directly. A common mistake is leaving a default constructor in the base creator so it can be instantiated; that can allow unexpected behavior at runtime. When you build an Abstract Factory, make sure every concrete factory implements all abstract factory methods; otherwise Python raises errors and your family contract is broken. Practice writing unit tests that ask a factory for a product and then assert the product implements the expected interface. Finally, think about when a factory is overkill: if you only ever have one concrete class and it will never change, direct instantiation is simpler. These checks help you apply patterns where they buy you extensibility, not complexity.

screens.title: What are Creational Patterns?
screens.subtitle: Define the goal: flexible, decoupled object creation

narration.text: Creational patterns group techniques for creating objects in a way that fits the situation, rather than letting client code construct concrete types directly. The core claim is simple: move knowledge of which concrete class to instantiate out of the client and into a dedicated place — a factory or creator — so that the rest of the system asks for behavior, not a specific implementation. For example, a document editor asks for a document that can open and save, not specifically a PDF or Word document object. A concrete example: if you directly call PdfDocument() across many modules, adding a new ExcelDocument requires changes everywhere. With a factory, you add a single creator for Excel and the client calls remain unchanged. A common misconception is that factories always add needless indirection; they do add a layer, but the benefit appears when types change, when testing needs mocks, or when you need to vary creation based on runtime configuration. Key takeaway: creational patterns trade a small upfront design cost for long-term extensibility and clearer separation of responsibilities. Can you find a place in your code where creation choices leak into business logic?

keyIdea.title: Creational pattern intent
keyIdea.text: Centralize instantiation so code depends on interfaces, not concrete classes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › What are Creational Patterns?

Definition

Creational patterns organize how objects are produced to reduce coupling and make systems easier to extend.

Concrete example

A document editor asks for a document interface. Different creators produce PdfDocument, WordDocument, or future ExcelDocument without modifying client code.

Common misconception

Factories add indirection but the payoff is maintenance and testability when types change or configuration varies at runtime.

Key takeaway

Centralize creation logic; depend on interfaces to respect the Open/Closed Principle.

Analogy

Factory as manufacturer

Think of a factory as a workshop that knows how to build products. The client places an order for a capability; the workshop picks the correct concrete tool to produce it.

Quick inspection prompt
  • Where in your code do constructors appear outside factories?
  • Would adding a new product require touching multiple modules?
  • Could tests use a factory to inject mocks instead of real objects?

screens.title: The Tight-Coupling Problem and Open/Closed Principle
screens.subtitle: Why scattered instantiation becomes a maintenance cost

narration.text: Let’s walk through the problem step by step so the solution feels natural. First, when client code directly calls concrete constructors, the client depends on the exact class names and parameters. For instance, many modules calling PdfDocument(filename) create a coupling to PDFs. Second, when a new type such as ExcelDocument is added, each place that created documents needs modification to decide which constructor to call. This is the maintenance step that breaks the Open/Closed Principle: the code is not closed for modification because adding a new product forces edits across the codebase. Third, scattered instantiation also harms testing. Tests that assume concrete constructors must manage real file input and output or setup, whereas factories let you substitute a mock product by swapping the factory. A simple process remedy is to centralize creation in a creator class with a single public create method. That method encapsulates the logic and delegates the specific build step to a private or abstract factory method. Misconception to avoid: centralizing creation does not mean hiding all variability. Expose configuration points where appropriate. Takeaway: centralizing creation reduces points of change and improves testability — what is one file you would refactor first to introduce a factory?

keyIdea.title: Process to reduce coupling
keyIdea.text: Centralize constructors in a creator; delegate specifics to factory methods to respect OCP and ease testing.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Tight Coupling & OCP
Problem steps
  1. Client constructs concrete types directly, creating tight dependencies.
  2. Adding a new product forces edits across modules that construct objects.
  3. Testing becomes harder because tests must manage concrete setup.
  4. Maintenance cost grows with each added product type.
Misconception

Factories are not a silver bullet. Use them when types vary or when families of products must stay consistent.

Remedy process
Create a Creator class

Expose a create method that encapsulates workflow and delegates to a factory method that subclasses override.

Use abstract product interfaces

Clients rely on methods like open and save, not on concrete class internals.

Add new types via new creators

Introduce ExcelCreator without touching client code that calls create.

Key Takeaway

Centralize construction and delegate specifics to preserve the Open/Closed Principle and simplify testing.

screens.title: Factory Method Pattern — Intent and Structure
screens.subtitle: Let subclasses choose which concrete product to create

narration.text: The Factory Method pattern defines a creator class with a factory method that subclasses implement to return the concrete product. The general structure includes a product interface, one or more concrete products, an abstract creator that contains a create workflow, and concrete creators that override the factory method to instantiate specific products. Concretely, our Document example has a Document abstract base class with open and save methods. PdfDocument and WordDocument implement that interface. DocumentCreator defines create_document, which calls an abstract _create_document factory method. PdfCreator overrides _create_document to return a PdfDocument. This separation means the client code invokes create_document and receives a ready-to-use product without knowing its class. A misconception is to make the factory method public and mix creation logic with business logic — keep the factory focused on construction and the creator method on orchestration. Example: adding ExcelDocument requires only adding ExcelCreator; no client changes. Takeaway: Factory Method is ideal when a single product hierarchy needs pluggable creation logic and subclasses should decide the concrete class. Factory Method Pattern — Intent and Structure means product interface, concrete products, abstract creator with factory method, and concrete creators implementing the factory.. In practical terms, let subclasses choose which concrete product to create. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Factory Method anatomy
keyIdea.text: Product interface, concrete products, abstract creator with factory method, and concrete creators implementing the factory.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Factory Method — Intent
Pattern structure
  • Product interface or abstract base class
  • Concrete products implementing the interface
  • Creator class with a public workflow method
  • Factory method (abstract) overridden by concrete creators
When to use

When a class wants subclasses to decide which concrete product to instantiate, often for a single product hierarchy.

Concrete example

DocumentCreator.create_document calls _create_document implemented by PdfCreator to return a PdfDocument. Client calls create_document and never sees the concrete class name.

Misconception

Avoid mixing creation and business concerns. Leave creation in the factory method and orchestration in the creator's public method.

Quick check

Can you add a new product by only creating a new concrete creator class?

screens.title: Factory Method — DocumentCreator Example (Python)
screens.subtitle: Read the code and observe how subclasses supply concrete products

narration.text: Now we step through a Python example that implements the Factory Method. The code defines a Document abstract base class with open and save methods. PdfDocument and WordDocument are concrete product classes that implement those methods and accept a filename in their constructors. DocumentCreator provides create_document which orchestrates the product lifecycle and calls the abstract _create_document factory method for the actual instantiation. PdfCreator and WordCreator override _create_document to return PdfDocument and WordDocument respectively. When the client uses PdfCreator. create_document('report. pdf'), the creator returns a product that responds to open and save. Note the concrete example shows printed messages to indicate creation and operations; in production you would avoid side effects inside constructors. A common mistake is leaving the base _create_document non-abstract permitting the base creator to be instantiated. This can cause runtime errors if code expects concrete behavior. Try to test factories by mocking the product interface to validate orchestration without hitting IO. The code panel below contains the full example for you to read and copy. In practical terms, read the code and observe how subclasses supply concrete products. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Factory Method in practice
keyIdea.text: The creator orchestrates lifecycle; concrete creators override the factory method to return specific products.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › DocumentCreator — Code
Code
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Document(ABC):
  @abstractmethod
  def open(self):
    pass

  @abstractmethod
  def save(self):
    pass

class PdfDocument(Document):
  def __init__(self, filename):
    self.filename = filename
    print(f"PDF Document '{filename}' created.")

  def open(self):
    print(f"Opening PDF: {self.filename}")

  def save(self):
    print(f"Saving PDF: {self.filename}")

class DocumentCreator(ABC):
  def create_document(self, filename):
    document = self._create_document(filename)
    document.open()
    document.save()
    return document

  @abstractmethod
  def _create_document(self, filename) -> Document:
    pass

class PdfCreator(DocumentCreator):
  def _create_document(self, filename) -> Document:
    return PdfDocument(filename)

# Client usage
pdf_creator = PdfCreator()
my_pdf = pdf_creator.create_document('report.pdf')
Explanation

The create_document workflow handles lifecycle calls such as open and save, while the factory method _create_document controls which concrete product is returned. This separation keeps orchestration code stable even when concrete products change.

  • Test orchestration by replacing the creator with a test double that returns a mock product.
  • Keep constructors free of heavy side effects to keep testing predictable.
  • Adding a new product requires only a new concrete product and creator.
Key Takeaway

Factory Method moves the decision of which concrete product to subclasses while preserving a stable workflow in the creator.

screens.title: Factory Method — Pitfalls and Tests
screens.subtitle: What often goes wrong and how to verify correctness

narration.text: When implementing the Factory Method, developers commonly make a few avoidable mistakes. One is leaving the base factory method as a concrete method with default behavior, which permits the abstract creator to be instantiated. That often surfaces as runtime errors when client code expects concrete behavior. Another mistake is placing side effects like file operations inside constructors. That couples creation time with resource access and makes tests brittle. Instead, move expensive setup out of constructors or wrap side effects behind methods that can be mocked. Regarding testing, verify both behavior and substitution. For behavior, assert that the returned product responds to required methods like open and save and that create_document orchestrates these calls. For substitution, replace the concrete factory in tests with a stub that returns a lightweight mock product. A concrete example: create a FakeDocument implementing open and save that records calls; inject a FakeCreator during tests and assert that create_document called open and save. Takeaway: construction logic should be explicit and testable. If you can’t test a factory without touching external resources, refactor until you can. Factory Method — Pitfalls and Tests means avoid instantiable abstract creators and side effects in constructors; use test doubles to verify orchestration.. In practical terms, what often goes wrong and how to verify correctness. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls & testing
keyIdea.text: Avoid instantiable abstract creators and side effects in constructors; use test doubles to verify orchestration.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Factory Method — Pitfalls

Common mistakes

  • Making the factory method concrete and instantiable.
  • Putting I/O or heavy side effects in constructors.
  • Mixing creation logic with domain orchestration.

Testing strategy

Replace the concrete creator with a fake that returns a lightweight product. Use a fake product that records calls to open and save, then assert that create_document invoked them. Keep constructors simple to allow instantiation without side effects.

Example test idea

Inject FakeCreator, call create_document, assert FakeDocument recorded open and save calls.

Pro tip

Mark factory methods abstract and keep constructors side-effect free to ease testing and maintainability.

screens.title: Implement Factory Method: Logger Factories (Starter Code)

narration.text: The hands-on activity asks you to implement the Factory Method to produce logger instances for different destinations. The starter code provides an abstract Logger with a log method, concrete ConsoleLogger and FileLogger, and an abstract LoggerFactory. Your task is to implement ConsoleLoggerFactory and FileLoggerFactory and then use them from client code. The FileLogger should accept a filename and append messages to a file. The point of this exercise is to practice delegating creation so client code calls create_logger and receives a logger without knowing its concrete type. A common trap is to let FileLogger perform heavy work in its constructor; instead, initialize file-related attributes and perform writes inside log. For testing, you can swap the factory to a fake factory that returns a logger that records messages. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Hands-on: Logger Factory
Starter Code
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

# 1. Abstract Product: Logger
class Logger(ABC):
  @abstractmethod
  def log(self, message: str):
    pass

# 2. Concrete Products: ConsoleLogger, FileLogger
class ConsoleLogger(Logger):
  def log(self, message: str):
    print(f"[CONSOLE] {message}")

class FileLogger(Logger):
  def __init__(self, filename: str):
    self.filename = filename
    print(f"FileLogger initialized for: {self.filename}")

  def log(self, message: str):
    with open(self.filename, 'a') as f:
      f.write(f"[FILE] {message}
")

# 3. Abstract Creator: LoggerFactory
class LoggerFactory(ABC):
  @abstractmethod
  def create_logger(self) -> Logger:
    pass

# 4. Concrete Creators: ConsoleLoggerFactory, FileLoggerFactory
# TODO: Implement ConsoleLoggerFactory
# TODO: Implement FileLoggerFactory

# 5. Client Code
if __name__ == "__main__":
  print("Using Console Logger:")
  console_factory = None  # TODO: Instantiate ConsoleLoggerFactory
  console_logger = console_factory.create_logger()
  console_logger.log("This is a console message.")

  print("
Using File Logger:")
  file_factory = None  # TODO: Instantiate FileLoggerFactory with a filename like 'app.log'
  file_logger = file_factory.create_logger()
  file_logger.log("This is a file message.")
Guidance & Example

Implement two simple factory classes: ConsoleLoggerFactory returns a ConsoleLogger instance, and FileLoggerFactory accepts a filename and returns a FileLogger with that filename. The client should construct a factory and call create_logger without importing concrete logger classes.

Testing tip

For unit tests, create a FakeFactory that returns a fake logger that records messages so you can assert calls without touching the file system.

Key Takeaway

Practice moving creation into factories so clients request behavior through an interface, not a concrete class.

screens.title: Abstract Factory Pattern — Intent and Use Case
screens.subtitle: Create families of related products with consistent themes

narration.text: The Abstract Factory pattern extends the idea of the Factory Method to families of related products. Instead of a single factory method that returns one product type, an Abstract Factory is an interface with multiple factory methods, each creating a different abstract product in the family. Concrete factories implement those methods to return platform-specific or theme-specific concrete products. For instance, a GUIFactory may have create_button and create_checkbox methods. WindowsGUIFactory returns Windows-style buttons and checkboxes while MacOSGUIFactory returns Mac O S-style components. The client asks the factory for a button and a checkbox and receives a consistent set of components without knowledge of their concrete classes. A key practicality is ensuring that concrete factories implement every factory method; forgetting one leads to runtime errors and breaks the family contract. Use Abstract Factory when products are designed to be used together and should match in style or representation. Misconception: Abstract Factory is not just multiple factories in one class; it enforces family consistency and is useful when families need to change together. Takeaway: Abstract Factory provides a single place to swap out entire product families.

keyIdea.title: Abstract Factory intent
keyIdea.text: Provide an interface to create related products so a client gets a coherent family without concrete class knowledge.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Abstract Factory — Intent
Pattern idea

Abstract Factory defines an interface for creating families of related objects. Concrete factories implement the interface to return theme-consistent products.

Example

GUIFactory.create_button and create_checkbox are implemented by WindowsGUIFactory and MacOSGUIFactory to produce consistent UI sets.

Common Pitfall

Adding a new product type to the abstract factory requires updating every concrete factory, which can be costly. Consider extending the hierarchy instead of changing the interface often.

When to choose
  • Your system needs families of related products that must be used together.
  • Platform or theme differences must be swapped as a whole.
  • Maintaining product consistency is a priority.
Key Takeaway

Abstract Factory is for producing coordinated product families so clients get a consistent set of implementations without referencing concrete classes.

screens.title: Abstract Factory — GUIFactory Example (Python)
screens.subtitle: See how factories produce families of components

narration.text: Let's examine the GUIFactory example that illustrates Abstract Factory. The code defines abstract product interfaces Button and Checkbox with paint methods, and concrete implementations like WindowsButton and MacOSButton that render platform-specific visuals. GUIFactory is the abstract factory with create_button and create_checkbox. WindowsGUIFactory and MacOSGUIFactory implement those methods to return corresponding concrete products. The client function application(factory) calls factory. create_button and factory. create_checkbox, then invokes paint on each product. The key idea is the client receives a coherent family of components from a single factory. A missed implementation of a factory method in a concrete factory will raise a TypeError or cause a mismatch in components. A practical example: switching from WindowsGUIFactory to MacOSGUIFactory changes the look of both buttons and checkboxes without any client code change. For testing, mock the factory to return lightweight objects that record paint calls. This pattern is particularly useful when product combinations must remain consistent across a UI or plugin environment. Abstract Factory — GUIFactory Example (Python) means concrete factories return matching sets of products so clients can swap product families by changing one factory.. In practical terms, see how factories produce families of components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Abstract Factory in practice
keyIdea.text: Concrete factories return matching sets of products so clients can swap product families by changing one factory.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › GUIFactory — Code
Code
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Button(ABC):
  @abstractmethod
  def paint(self):
    pass

class WindowsButton(Button):
  def paint(self):
    print("Rendering a button in Windows style.")

class MacOSButton(Button):
  def paint(self):
    print("Rendering a button in macOS style.")

class Checkbox(ABC):
  @abstractmethod
  def paint(self):
    pass

class WindowsCheckbox(Checkbox):
  def paint(self):
    print("Rendering a checkbox in Windows style.")

class MacOSCheckbox(Checkbox):
  def paint(self):
    print("Rendering a checkbox in macOS style.")

class GUIFactory(ABC):
  @abstractmethod
  def create_button(self) -> Button:
    pass

  @abstractmethod
  def create_checkbox(self) -> Checkbox:
    pass

class WindowsGUIFactory(GUIFactory):
  def create_button(self) -> Button:
    return WindowsButton()

  def create_checkbox(self) -> Checkbox:
    return WindowsCheckbox()

class MacOSGUIFactory(GUIFactory):
  def create_button(self) -> Button:
    return MacOSButton()

  def create_checkbox(self) -> Checkbox:
    return MacOSCheckbox()

def application(factory: GUIFactory):
  button = factory.create_button()
  checkbox = factory.create_checkbox()
  button.paint()
  checkbox.paint()

application(WindowsGUIFactory())
application(MacOSGUIFactory())
Explanation

The client function expects only a GUIFactory. Each concrete factory supplies a set of products that match in style. Swapping the factory swaps the whole family and keeps client code unchanged.

  • Ensure each concrete factory implements every abstract factory method.
  • When adding a new product type, you must update all concrete factories — consider design costs before expanding the abstract interface.
  • Mock factories in tests to verify application behavior without rendering real UI.
Key Takeaway

Abstract Factory bundles creation methods so clients receive a consistent family of products; use when product sets must remain coherent.

screens.title: Factory Method vs Abstract Factory
screens.subtitle: Compare scope, intent, and when to use each pattern

narration.text: Understanding the difference between the Factory Method and the Abstract Factory is essential when designing extensible systems. The Factory Method focuses on a single product hierarchy: an abstract creator delegates the choice of concrete class to subclasses via a factory method. Use it when a class wants subclasses to decide which product to create. The Abstract Factory focuses on families of related products: an interface exposes multiple factory methods, and concrete factories return coherent sets of products. Use it when multiple related objects must be produced together and remain consistent. A helpful contrast: if you need only one product that varies, Factory Method is simpler and less intrusive. If you need buttons, checkboxes, and text fields all to change together by theme or platform, Abstract Factory is appropriate. A typical misconception is to treat Abstract Factory as merely several Factory Methods grouped together; its real power is guaranteeing family consistency. Concrete example: DocumentCreator is Factory Method; GUIFactory is Abstract Factory. Takeaway: match pattern scope to your problem — single product variability versus coordinated families. Factory Method vs Abstract Factory means factory method for single product variability; abstract factory for families of related products that must remain consistent.. In practical terms, compare scope, intent, and when to use each pattern. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern selection
keyIdea.text: Factory Method for single product variability; Abstract Factory for families of related products that must remain consistent.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Factory Method vs Abstract Factory

Factory Method

  • Scope: single product hierarchy
  • Structure: abstract creator + factory method
  • Use when subclasses decide concrete classes

Abstract Factory

  • Scope: families of related products
  • Structure: abstract factory interface with multiple creation methods
  • Use when product sets must remain consistent
Concrete examples
Factory Method: DocumentCreator → PdfCreator, WordCreator
Abstract Factory: GUIFactory → WindowsGUIFactory, MacOSGUIFactory

narration.text: When selecting a pattern, weigh the frequency and scope of expected changes. If you anticipate only a few new concrete products in a single hierarchy, Factory Method keeps complexity low while still providing extensibility. If you expect sets of related products to vary together across environments or themes, Abstract Factory reduces coupling between product families and clients. Consider the maintenance burden: adding a product to an Abstract Factory requires updating every concrete factory, which may be costly if you have many platforms. In that case, you might combine patterns or evolve the factory interface slowly. Also think about testing and configuration: factories are ideal places to inject dependencies, perform lazy creation, or apply configuration-based selection at startup. A hybrid approach sometimes fits: use Factory Method to choose a concrete factory, and let that factory be an Abstract Factory that returns product families. Misconception: complexity alone is not a reason to avoid patterns; the right pattern balances immediate simplicity with long-term adaptability. Closing question: which pattern reduces future churn for your current project? Choosing Between Patterns and Extensions means choose by scope of variability: single-product changes favor factory method; coordinated multi-product changes favor abstract factory.. keyIdea.title: Design trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Choose by scope of variability: single-product changes favor Factory Method; coordinated multi-product changes favor Abstract Factory.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Choosing a Pattern
Decision factors
  • Scope of variability: single product vs family
  • Maintenance cost: how many concrete factories will you update?
  • Testing needs: can you inject test factories or mocks?
  • Configuration: will factories be selected at runtime?
Patterns can combine

You can use a Factory Method to select which Abstract Factory to use, allowing a two-stage decision: which family, then which product within that family.

Practical tip

Start with the simplest pattern that meets your needs. Refactor to more complex patterns only when families or platform differences demand it.

narration.text: These are the compact ideas to keep in mind as you apply creational patterns. First, creational patterns centralize object creation so client code depends on abstract interfaces rather than concrete classes. Second, Factory Method delegates the decision of which concrete product to subclasses through a factory method and fits single-product hierarchies. Third, Abstract Factory produces families of related products via an interface of multiple creation methods, ensuring the client gets a consistent set of components. Each concept reduces coupling and increases extensibility when used appropriately. As a quick self-test, name one place in your code where constructors are scattered, and imagine replacing them with a creator or factory. Factory Method

Final takeaway

Design factories to centralize creation points, reduce coupling, and make adding new types a simple extension rather than a code-wide change.

narration.text: Keep these three concise cards handy as you code. First, product versus creator: products implement behavior and creators are responsible for producing them. Second, Factory Method: a creator delegates the choice of a single product to subclasses using a factory method; this is ideal for single-product hierarchies and for letting subclasses vary products without changing client orchestration. Third, Abstract Factory: a factory interface exposes several creation methods to produce a family of related products; switching concrete factories swaps an entire product family consistently. A practical prompt: before refactoring, name the product interfaces and the likely creators for your codebase. That quick exercise helps you apply these patterns where they will reduce future churn.
